controlling: {leader} doesn't sit. “We're voting for {bill}, all of us, and I'd like that to be the shortest item on today's agenda.”
{leader} hands out a single page of talking points on {bill}. “These are the words. Please use these words.”
“I've read every amendment to {bill}, including the ones you were thinking of moving,” {leader} says. “We support it as written.”
{leader} taps the table twice. “{bill} is whipped. {whip} will be taking attendance, and so will I.”
“There will be no free vote on {bill},” {leader} says, before anyone has asked for one.
handsOff: {leader} reads the agenda aloud, gets to {bill}, and looks at {whip}. “I gather we're supporting this. Any thoughts?”
“I'm not going to tell you how to feel about {bill},” {leader} says. “{whip} will tell you how to vote.”
{leader} arrives four minutes late with a coffee. “{bill}. We're for it, broadly. Let's hear from the room.”
“I trust this caucus,” {leader} says, which everyone knows means {whip} has already done the count on {bill}.
{leader} leans back. “The line on {bill} is support. If that's a problem for anyone, talk to {whip}, not the press.”
paranoid: {leader} closes the door personally and checks it. “What's said about {bill} in this room ends up in the paper. I'd like to know how.”
“Someone told the gallery we were split on {bill},” {leader} says. “We are not split. We are voting yes.”
{leader} looks down the table one face at a time. “I'll know who's with me on {bill} by Thursday night.”
“Phones in the basket,” {leader} says. {whip} walks the basket around. Then: “Now. {bill}.”
{leader} says the line on {bill} is support, then adds, to no one in particular, that loyalty is noticed.
loyal: {leader} stands. “{bill} is a hard vote for some of you, and I know who. I'm asking you to trust me on this one.”
“Some of your ridings won't love {bill},” {leader} says. “When they ask, send them to me. That's my job, not yours.”
{leader} thanks the caucus for the last vote, by name, before turning to {bill}. “We're for it. Let's carry it together.”
“I've never asked this caucus for more than it could give,” {leader} says. “I'm asking for {bill}.”
{leader} sets the line on {bill} and promises to visit every riding that pays a price for it. A few people write that down.

grievances.text: {name} stands up and complains that {riding} found out about {bill} from the evening news.
{name} stands up and complains that the leader's office rewrote their press release and spelled {riding} wrong.
{name} stands up and complains that {leader} hasn't set foot in their province since the campaign bus left.
{name} stands up and complains that the platform promised one thing and {bill} does the opposite.
{name} stands up and complains that every decision now gets made by three staffers under thirty.
{name} stands up and complains that caucus is told the line rather than asked about it.
{name} stands up and complains that {leader} took questions from the gallery before taking them from caucus.
{name} stands up and complains that {whip} denied their travel to a funeral in {riding} and approved {other}'s trip to a conference.
{name} stands up and complains that the whip's office called their spouse looking for them.
{name} stands up and complains that they've been on House duty four Fridays in a row while {other} hasn't done one.
{name} stands up and complains that {whip} keeps a file on everyone and they'd like to see theirs.
{name} stands up and complains that their Question Period slot was given away without a phone call.
{name} stands up and complains that the whip's office threatened their committee seat over a tweet.
{name} stands up and complains that pairs are being handed out like party favours to the leader's friends.
{name} stands up and complains that the transport minister hasn't returned a call about {riding} since March.
{name} stands up and complains that cabinet announced money in {riding} without inviting its MP.
{name} stands up and complains that ministers treat backbenchers like a studio audience.
{name} stands up and complains that the department wrote {bill} without asking anyone who'd ever lived outside Ostrava.
{name} stands up and complains that a minister's chief of staff hung up on their constituency assistant.
{name} stands up and complains that cabinet is drawn entirely from three provinces and it shows.
{name} stands up and complains that {other} briefed the press on {bill} before caucus had seen it.
{name} stands up and complains that the parking passes for the precinct have been reassigned again.
{name} stands up and complains that {other} has been fundraising in {riding} without asking.
{name} stands up and complains that the research bureau's polling on {bill} has been sitting in a drawer.
{name} stands up and complains that the caucus coffee is, and has always been, undrinkable.
{name} stands up and complains that {other} voted against the line last month and nothing happened to them.

stances.text: Back the line on {bill}. We win this one together or not at all.
Thank the leader for the briefing and say you'll carry {bill} in your riding.
Remind the room that the opposition would love nothing more than a split vote.
Say {bill} isn't perfect, but it's ours, and you'll vote for it.
Tell them what {bill} costs your riding, with the numbers, and ask for a fix.
Read out a letter from a constituent, word for word, and sit down.
Say you'll vote for it if your riding gets the amendment. Otherwise, you can't.
Ask that the next riding announcement go to a seat that paid for this vote.
Ask why caucus is told the line instead of asked. Loudly.
Say you won't vote for {bill} as written, and that you suspect you're not alone.
Ask the whip, in front of everyone, what happens to members who vote their riding.
Move that {bill} be a free vote. Ask for a show of hands.
Say nothing. Take notes. Watch who's sitting with whom.
Nod when the leader speaks and leave before the grievances.
Stay seated, but catch the whip after the meeting with your concerns.
Pass a note down the table and let someone braver read it out.

whispers.text: “Say the word and I'll back you up if you speak. I owe you one from last month.”
“{whip} is in a good mood today. If you want something, ask before the vote, not after.”
“{name} wants to get a group of rookies together for dinner. You should come.”
“{leader} actually listens when it's about a riding. Ask about yours.”
“I'm voting for {bill}, but I'd sit next to you if you didn't.”
“Careful what you say about {bill} today. Half this table talks to the gallery.”
“I've heard things about {other}. I'll tell you later. Not here.”
“Don't look now, but {whip} is writing down who claps.”
“I'm keeping my head down this week. I'd suggest you do the same.”
“Whatever {name} is about to say, I'm not with them. Officially.”
“If {leader} says ‘team’ one more time, I'm walking out.”
“{whip} cancelled my pair an hour before the vote. An hour. I had a daughter's recital.”
“There are eight of us who won't vote for {bill}. Nine, if you're interested.”
“{other} got the riding announcement I was promised. Ask yourself who's next.”
“I didn't win my seat by forty votes to be a yes on {bill}.”
“If {bill} goes the wrong way, does that trigger an election? Nobody will give me a straight answer.”
“My riding association president has started returning other people's calls.”
“Do you think {whip} knows about the thing? You know the thing.”
“I'm four points down at home and I just got asked to vote for {bill}.”
“{name} says there's a shuffle coming. Are you hearing that? Is it bad?”

calm: The room is quiet. Someone is passing around a birthday card, and most people are signing it.
People are reading the agenda instead of each other. The coffee is gone by the second item.
The cliques sit where they always sit, and nobody is leaning across the table.
A few laughs at the leader's joke, more than it deserved. Nobody wants a fight today.
restless: Chairs creak. The back end of the table is whispering more than it's listening.
Two members from the same province have their heads together, and they stop when the whip looks over.
Someone asks a procedural question that is not really a procedural question.
The applause after the leader's remarks starts on time and ends early.
angry: Nobody claps. The silence after the leader sits down goes on long enough to be counted.
Three people stand to speak at once, and the chair has to pick one.
The whip has stopped taking notes and started counting heads.
Someone says “with respect,” which in this room means the opposite.
